common_name: Burgundy Rubber Tree (Black Prince Rubber Plant)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained potting mix; Burgundy holds its darkest color with consistent bright indirect light and needs protection from direct hot sun, which can scorch the thick leaves.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained potting mix, letting the top inch or two dry out between waterings. Burgundy is a solid-color sport of the classic rubber tree carrying large, thick, glossy leaves that emerge coppery-red and mature to a deep, near-black burgundy, an intense wine-dark color that reads almost black in lower light and takes on warmer red highlights when the plant gets brighter light. Unlike the variegated Ruby and Tineke cultivars, its color comes from pigment rather than variegated tissue, so it grows a bit more vigorously and is somewhat more tolerant of average indoor light while still needing brightness to hold its darkest hue. Wipe dust from the broad leaves periodically to keep pores clear, stake or prune tall canes to control height, and protect from cold drafts and temperatures below 55°F, which can trigger leaf drop.

planting.note: Root stem or leaf-bud cuttings, or purchase container stock, and place in bright, indirect light in well-drained potting mix; Bambino is far more tolerant of average room conditions and tighter spaces than the full-sized species, but still dislikes being moved once settled.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect light indoors or in filtered shade outdoors in zones 10-12, allowing the top 2 inches of potting mix to dry between waterings. Bambino is a naturally compact, shrubby selection of fiddle-leaf fig that produces the same glossy, deeply veined, violin-shaped leaves as the species but on a densely branching plant that tops out at a fraction of the size, staying a manageable tabletop or floor accent rather than growing into a room-filling tree. Its smaller leaves and shorter internodes make it noticeably more forgiving of the lower light and tighter footprint of an average home or apartment than standard fiddle-leaf fig. Clean the leaves periodically with a damp cloth to keep them glossy, avoid cold drafts and sudden relocation, and rotate the pot occasionally so growth stays even on all sides.

planting.note: Establish container plants in bright, indirect light in well-drained potting mix; Starlight needs brighter light than plain-green weeping fig to maintain its white variegation and is prone to leaf drop after any sudden change in light, temperature, or watering.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect light as a houseplant or, in frost-free zones 10-12, in filtered shade outdoors, keeping soil evenly moist but letting the surface dry slightly between waterings. Starlight is among the most heavily variegated of the weeping fig cultivars, with small, pointed, glossy leaves boldly margined and often mostly overlaid in creamy white around a deep green center, giving the graceful, arching branches a noticeably brighter, frostier look than plain green Ficus benjamina. Because the pale leaf tissue does less photosynthetic work, Starlight grows more slowly and needs more consistent bright light than the species to avoid reverting toward green and to prevent thin, sparse growth. Like all weeping figs it drops leaves readily in response to drafts, relocation, or changes in watering, so choose a permanent, stable spot and avoid moving it once established.

planting.note: Root 3-4 inch stem cuttings in water or moist potting mix; cuttings root in 1-2 weeks. Quadricolor needs brighter light than plain zebrina to hold its full range of leaf color and can revert toward plain silver-green stripes in low light.

directions: Root cuttings in water and transplant to moist, well-drained soil in partial to bright shade. Quadricolor layers additional pink and cream striping over the silver-and-green banding of standard wandering jew, so each leaf can show four distinct colors at once — deep green, silver, cream, and rose-pink — over the same rich purple leaf underside as the species, making it noticeably showier than plain Tradescantia zebrina. It shares the same fast-spreading, easy-rooting habit as its parent species and works well as a hanging basket trailer or shaded groundcover in zones 9-11, though it is somewhat slower and less vigorous than the plain green-and-silver form. Give it the brightest indirect light the space allows to keep the pink tones from fading, pinch stems to keep growth compact, and handle with care since the sap can cause skin irritation in sensitive individuals.

planting.note: Divide rosette offsets or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained soil in partial shade after the last frost; Tricolor needs brighter light than the plain green-and-purple species to maintain its cream and pink striping and can revert to solid color in deep shade.

directions: Divide rosette offsets or plant container specimens in well-drained soil in partial shade, allowing the soil to dry somewhat between waterings. Tricolor carries the same stiff, lance-shaped rosettes and rich purple leaf undersides as plain oyster plant, but each upper leaf surface is striped lengthwise in cream, soft pink, and green rather than solid dark green, giving established clumps a much brighter, more decorative presence in a shaded bed or container. The variegation is most vivid in bright, indirect light and fades toward plain green in deep shade, so give it a lighter spot than the species while still avoiding direct hot sun, which can scorch the thinner variegated tissue. Like the species it is tough and drought-tolerant once established and spreads slowly by offsets, which can be divided to propagate or control spread; it is root-hardy to around 25-28°F in zone 9 even where top growth is lost to frost.
